newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Komineft sees 1998 profit on restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Komineft sees 1998 profit on restructuring.

text.p: Russian oil company Komineft, beset by problems common to much of the country's oil industry, is tackling some of them head on and says it could soon see some positive results.

The main production unit of KomiTEK, a vertically integrated oil company set up in 1995 to include both the Ukhta refinery and Kominefteprodukt, Komineft is based in a vast northwestern region rich in natural resources.

But like many other companies, it is struggling to pay off tax arrears, streamline its cumbersome Soviet structure, and to find trillions of roubles in investment for new oil field exploration and development.

While a 1994 oil spill near the northern town of Usinsk has long ago been cleaned up, Komineft is still paying off about $124 million lent by the World Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) to replace the pipe.

Nevertheless, deputy director general Vitaly Pinchuk says the company, which last year posted a 254 billion rouble ($44.1 million) pre-tax loss, could settle up on its government debt and even see profits in 1998 if restructuring work is completed.
"In 1997, there probably won't be any (profit) because, and I stress, we haven't yet finished restructuring," he told Reuters in an interview.
"But in 1998, if we put all our effort into it, I think we could come out with a profit. Maybe net profit -- maybe."
Pinchuk said Komineft was spinning off non-core enterprises, such as transport, supply and farming. It was also cutting both a bloated workforce and burdensome tax obligations.
The number of employees would be cut almost in half by the end of 1997, slimming to a near-optimum 9-10,000 from 18,000 at the beginning of the year, he said.
Pinchuk said Komineft would be saddled with servicing the World Bank and EBRD loan until 2009. But he played down their importance in the overall scheme of company finances.
"It's taking a toll and will continue to have an effect for a long time, until we pay off the money," he said. "Twelve to 16 million dollars a year -- that's a handsome sum, but not a fatal one."
Despite the activity, however, much remains to be done.
Pinchuk said the company will need serious investment to pump up production figures, which have plummeted to 3.5 million tonnes a year from 18 million in the mid-1980s, he said.
Some of that decline, he said, was due to allocating oil wells to joint ventures and the separation of some companies from Komineft, as in the case of a small firm called Tebukneft.
Komineft even managed to raise production in 1996 by around 100-150,000 tonnes by tapping idle wells, he said.
But for significant growth in output, not only idle wells must be relaunched, which itself requires money, but new wells must be drilled and new oil deposits explored, Pinchuk said.
"The programme that we've worked up currently calls for 300 billion roubles ($52.1 million) a year -- but that's a bare minimum," he said.
"We would need around 600-700 billion roubles ($100-120 million) to give life to old wells and drill new ones. I'm not including in that the investment needed to find new deposits."
But Pinchuk talks of the future in an optimistic tone.
"Our main problem is that our expenditures don't fit into our revenues," he said.
"Our main task is to finish restructuring," he said. "Once we have cut ourselves down to a minimum and brought...our numbers into line, we'll be a little compact company."
